While the basic premise—a working-class woman marrying a wealthy man with an intimidating mother—sets up expectations for a familiar, cliché plot, the story actively subverts those tropes at every turn. 

Instead of being a dashing billionaire, Teddy is "soft in the middle" with a face only relatives have called handsome, and he harbors no jealousy or resentment when his mother favors his wife over him in the family business. Instead of being a two-dimensional, malicious villain trying to break the couple up, Miss Emily is a complex, self-made businesswoman whose scrutiny isn't born of cruelty, but of a lifelong habit of "taking inventory." Even the resolution avoids the cliché of the protagonist either completely conforming to high society or rebelliously rejecting it; instead, Marnie finds a nuanced middle ground built on mutual utility and quiet self-respect. Furthermore, the prose itself relies on fresh, specific metaphors and observations rather than tired, overused expressions.
